messages.author: e76612751d0fd653
messages.subject: ERRORS IN MULTI GROUP CFA
parts:
I have 100 datasets that have been multiply imputed. They are already imputed and I cannot use mice or amelia impute them. I am trying to run a mult-group CFA to compare males and females. In order to tell R that I have 100 datasets (not 2500 girls) I ran the following:

nImputations <- 100
impList <- list() 
for (i in as.numeric(names(table(Testing2$Imputation)))) 
{impList[[i]] <- Testing2[Testing2$Imputation == i , ]}

This seems to work. I then attempted to make the list a data.frame by running:

sapply(impList, is.atomic)
sapply(impList, length)
all(sapply(impList, is.atomic)) # should be TRUE
all(sapply(impList, length) == sapply(impList, length)[1]) # should be TRUE

IMPLISTDF <- as.data.frame(impList)

It created a dataset with 371 observations of 22000 variables. A problem that I ran into with this was all(sapply(impList, is.atomic)) was FALSE not TRUE. 

In attempting to run my cfa I used the following script:

FMLQ1test <- (OV =~ w1otv1 + w1otv2 + w1otv3
              OE =~ w1ote1 + w1ote2 + w1ote3
              GA =~ w1oara1 + w1oara2 + w1oara3
              GV =~ w1ovrv1 + w1ovrv2 + w1ovrv3 + w1oara1 
              PA =~ RES_pa + w1oara2 
              PV =~ RES_pv + w1ovrv2
              REA =~ RES_rea
              REV =~ RES_rev
              w1oara1 ~~ w1oara2)

out <- runMI(FMLQ1test, data=IMPLISTDF, chi="mplus", group="w1gender", fun="cfa") 

I get the following error:

Error in eigen(Sigma.hat[[g]], symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE) : 
  infinite or missing values in 'x'

The variables in the model, as well at the gender variable, have 0 missing data. So I am not sure why it is telling that it cannot compute the eigen values. 
I have tried many many different ways to fix this, including just trying to run measurement invariance with the data.frame I created. 

Any tips as soon as possible would be incredibly appreciated.

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: ERRORS IN MULTI GROUP CFA
parts:
I then attempted to make the list a data.frame by running:

sapply(impList, is.atomic)
sapply(impList, length)
all(sapply(impList, is.atomic)) # should be TRUE
all(sapply(impList, length) == sapply(impList, length)[1]) # should be TRUE

IMPLISTDF <- as.data.frame(impList)

It created a dataset with 371 observations of 22000 variables. A problem that I ran into with this was all(sapply(impList, is.atomic)) was FALSE not TRUE.

Don't do that :-)  The message where you found this syntax had nothing to do with multiple imputation.  Someone's (I assume complete) data was in the form of a list of vectors rather than a data.frame that lavaan expects.  So this syntax creates a single data frame from a list of individual vectors (i.e., individual columns in a data set).

You are using the runMI() function to fit a model to data that have already been imputed 100 times, so you need to keep those 100 data frames in the form of a list, and pass that list of data directly to runMI()

out <- runMI(FMLQ1test, data=impList, chi="mplus", group="w1gender", fun="cfa") 

Terry

parts:
If you can provide more information about why the model "does not work" with other chi-square options (e.g. error messages), we may be able to decode things.

The mr and mplus chi squares (which are identical) are considerably more computationally intensive than the lmrr chi square so there are several possible ways things may have gone wrong.

Alex

messages.author: 5d4f9e7f97c21008
messages.subject: Re: ERRORS IN MULTI GROUP CFA
parts:
To see information about model convergence across data sets, use inspect(object, what = "impute") 

This will give you the convergence rate of the imputed data sets across your imputations (the proportion of imputations with models that converged) along with other information from the imputations (e.g. fraction of missing information for each parameter). 

The error message you see with chi="mplus" may come from the parameter estimates in your model. Check all the (combined) parameter estimates in your model to make sure they make sense. It may also come from the data sets, without more information on the data and how it was imputed, this is difficult to determine.
